- If sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is strongly negative (≤-0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — consider slight upward correction.  
- When true outcome spikes sharply after a low, model often underreacts — adjust forecast to include a slight lagged overshoot.  
- If history shows mean reversion (e.g., recent prices near 70–75) and sentiment is neutral, forecast should not drift too far from recent mean.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from 30-day moving average of history, reweight forecast toward recent data.  
- If sentiment history shows rising optimism but price is flat or falling, model may be overconfident — dampen forecast growth.  
- If forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp upward movement, consider a “sudden spike” correction rule: add 2–3% buffer to forecast if sentiment >0.6.  
- If sentiment is high but price drops sharply, model may be overfitting — apply a “sentiment decay” rule: reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day if sentiment >0.7 and price falls.
